<p>Most early-stage startups run into the same wall: there’s more work than people to do it. Engineering, product, research, marketing, operations — each function demands attention, but a founding team of one or two can’t be everywhere at once.</p>
<p>Gary Tan, president of Y Combinator, built GStack as a direct response to that constraint. It’s an open-source framework that structures Claude Code — Anthropic’s agentic AI coding tool — so a solo developer can handle work across multiple startup functions in a single session. GStack doesn’t add a new interface or product on top of Claude. It gives Claude better instructions, organized around what a startup actually needs to do.</p>
<p>This article explains what GStack is, how it works technically, and what kind of developer it’s designed for.</p>
<h2 id="gary-tan-y-combinator-and-why-this-framework-matters">Gary Tan, Y Combinator, and Why This Framework Matters</h2>

<p>GStack is his personal project, not an official YC or Anthropic product. He published it on GitHub under an open-source license, which means anyone can use it, fork it, or contribute to it.</p>

<h2 id="what-claude-code-actually-does">What Claude Code Actually Does</h2>
<p>Before understanding GStack, it helps to understand what Claude Code is and why it’s different from a standard AI chat interface.</p>
<p><a href="https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code">Claude Code</a> is Anthropic’s terminal-based AI agent. You run it from the command line, point it at a project, and it operates directly in your development environment. It can read and write files, run bash commands, execute tests, make git commits, call APIs, and work through multi-step tasks autonomously.</p>
<p>The key difference from a code completion tool or a chat assistant is that Claude Code takes actions rather than just making suggestions. It doesn’t wait for you to copy-paste its output — it applies changes directly, runs the results, and continues from there.</p>
<p>This makes it genuinely agentic. A single Claude Code session can write a feature, test it, debug the failures, commit the result, and move to the next task. For a solo developer, that’s meaningful leverage.</p>
<p>GStack is built specifically on top of this agentic behavior. The framework works because Claude Code can read context files, maintain state across a session, and apply different modes of reasoning to different kinds of tasks.</p>
<h2 id="inside-gstack-how-the-framework-is-structured">Inside GStack: How the Framework Is Structured</h2>
<p>GStack is a GitHub repository containing a structured collection of files that configure how Claude Code thinks and acts throughout a project. The central mechanism is the CLAUDE.md file — a markdown document that Claude Code reads automatically at the start of every session.</p>
<h3 id="how-claudemd-files-work">How CLAUDE.md Files Work</h3>
<p>When Claude Code starts a session, it scans the project directory for a file named CLAUDE.md. If it finds one, it reads the content as persistent context before doing anything else. This context shapes how Claude approaches every task in that session.</p>
<p>CLAUDE.md files can contain:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Project context</strong> — what the product does, who the users are, what the tech stack looks like</li>
<li><strong>Behavioral instructions</strong> — how Claude should prioritize decisions, what it should flag for human review</li>
<li><strong>Workflow patterns</strong> — step-by-step processes for recurring tasks</li>
<li><strong>Constraints</strong> — things Claude should never do without explicit approval</li>
</ul>
<p>Claude Code supports nested CLAUDE.md files. A root-level file sets the overall project context. Subdirectory files add more specific context relevant to the code or work in that directory. Claude reads all of them relevant to the current task, building a layered understanding of what the project is and what it should be doing.</p>
<h3 id="role-aware-workflows">Role-Aware Workflows</h3>
<p>What GStack adds is a set of CLAUDE.md files structured around startup roles rather than just engineering tasks. The framework includes specialized instruction sets for:</p>
<p><strong>Engineering</strong> — Architecture decisions, code review standards, when to refactor vs. ship, how to handle technical debt responsibly.</p>
<p><strong>Product</strong> — How to think through user problems, how to write specs that translate directly into executable tasks, how to evaluate feature priority.</p>
<p><strong>Research</strong> — How to synthesize competitive information, how to evaluate sources, how to turn raw data into a clear recommendation.</p>
<p><strong>Operations</strong> — Patterns for handling customer feedback, documenting decisions, managing project state, and maintaining internal documentation.</p>
